About
We measure reef gear so you don’t have to guess.
ReefMetric is an independent, reader-supported resource for saltwater aquarium keepers. We pair published manufacturer and retailer specifications with sizing calculations and side-by-side comparisons so you can choose equipment for your actual tank.
How we rate
Every recommendation starts with the numbers that matter for your tank: skimmer rating vs. bioload, pump flow vs. head loss, PAR vs. depth. Our current comparisons use published specs and calculated estimates. They are not first-hand bench tests. Read
how we rate reef gear
to see the methods and limits.
How we stay independent
We earn affiliate commissions when you buy through our links, at no extra cost to you. That never changes what we recommend — our rankings are driven by the data, not the payout.
Read our full disclosure
.
What the tools help you decide
A pump that looks large enough on its box may deliver less water once it has to lift it through your plumbing. The
return pump calculator
estimates that loss and compares the result with pump curves. The
skimmer size calculator
adjusts capacity for stocking and lets you check whether the body fits your sump. Both help narrow a buying list; neither can measure conditions inside your own aquarium.
The
reef lighting review
separates fixtures with published PAR data from those without it. The
reef tank cost calculator
puts equipment and running expenses in one place so you can see what a build leaves out before you order.
How to check a recommendation
Start with your tank's water volume, available equipment space, and the coral and fish you plan to keep. Follow the source links beside product data, check the date, and confirm the current model and price with the retailer. A different pump revision, mount height, or sump water level can change the answer. Estimates are starting points, not guarantees of a particular result.

Apex vs HYDROS vs GHL: reef tank controller comparison
Choose Apex when its expansion hardware fits your plan, HYDROS when its app-based control and modular kits fit, or GHL ProfiLux when you want its probe bundle and logic programming. Compare the complete kit, not just the controller's entry price: a bare brain or monitor is not the same purchase as a package with controllable outlets.

Budget & DIY-friendly controllers
Not every reefer needs — or wants to pay for — an $800+ flagship kit. Two names come up constantly in that budget/DIY conversation. One is a real, current, actively developed option. The other is a cautionary tale worth knowing before you buy one used.
Where it wins
Cheapest complete kit on this page — $399 includes the relay box, probes, and float switches with nothing extra required to get running
Fully open-source (Arduino) — public source code and hardware schematics, a real point of difference from every closed ecosystem above
Built-in WiFi on the Star — the earlier RA+ needed a separate add-on module
Actively maintained — GitHub commits into December 2025, still a going concern (unlike some DIY-era peers, see ReefKeeper below)
Where it hurts
Smallest third-party ecosystem here — no automated water-testing hardware exists for it (no Trident/ION Director equivalent)
No native dosing pump — relay outlets can switch a third-party doser on/off but can't program a dose volume
Full customization requires real Arduino/C++ comfort — the wizard covers the basics, but the 'open and hackable' pitch cuts both ways
Smallest community and support footprint of any current (non-discontinued) option on this page

Probes: temp, pH · 8-port relay box + 2 float-switch inputs included; 3 temperature channels total (1 probe in the box, more sold separately)

What about ReefKeeper?
Digital Aquatics' ReefKeeper (RK1, ReefKeeper Lite, ReefKeeper Elite/Elite Plus) built a loyal following over more than a decade, and owners still describe the hardware as rock-solid. It's also
completely discontinued
. Digital Aquatics was a side project of Dynon Instruments, an avionics company — Dynon exited the aquarium-controller business entirely, so there are no new units, no firmware updates, and no manufacturer support. As of 2026-07-01, digitalaquatics.com itself redirects to a GoDaddy domain-parking page — about as final a signal as a shutdown gets.
If you already own one, the hardware generally keeps running locally, but don't expect app updates or help if something breaks. Bulk Reef Supply occasionally lists open-box ReefKeeper stock — a fine cheap secondhand buy with your eyes open, but it's old dead stock, not a supported product. Buying new today, you're better served by Reef Angel above for a budget/DIY build, or by Apex, HYDROS, or GHL — all three compared in full
further up this page
.
Which one fits your build?
First controller on a 40–90 gallon mixed reef, and you want it to just work:
HYDROS. The X4/XP8 Pro Pack at $820.04 undercuts the equivalent Apex by ~$350, Collectives won't fight you, and the mesh design means an outlet-bar failure doesn't kill the brain. Budget for expansion hardware separately; use the testing row and manufacturer links above to check the setup you need.
SPS-focused tank where automated Alk testing is the point:
Apex. Trident is the reason — it's the most proven auto-tester, and the Apex ecosystem (DOS, third-party gear, a decade of Reef2Reef threads for every problem) is unmatched. Buy the full A3, not the Jr, and run Ethernet to it on day one.
You calibrate probes for fun and want the most capable machine:
GHL. Nothing else ships four lab-grade probes with calibration fluids in the box, ION Director tests five parameters with zero recurring reagent cost, and logic gates will do things the other two can't. Budget real learning time — the $997.90 Mega-Set is the on-ramp.
You're an engineer with more time than money:
Open-source Raspberry Pi controller (actively maintained, May 2026 commits). Automates ATO, temp, lighting, dosing, pH for roughly $150 in parts — zero warranty, zero support, real time investment.
Reef-Pi on GitHub ↗
FAQ
Before adding a controller, check which jobs the tank actually needs. The
auto top-off comparison
covers standalone overfill protection, and the
reef dosing pump rankings
show which pumps need a separate controller. Include those extra parts in the kit cost.
Does Apex Fusion, myGHL, or the HYDROS app charge a monthly fee?
No — as of 2026-07-01, all three clouds are free. Apex Fusion, myGHL/GHL Connect, and the HYDROS app have no subscription tier. The recurring costs that ARE real: Trident reagents (~$45 every 2 months) if you add automated testing to an Apex.
Which reef controller is easiest to program?
HYDROS. Its Collectives system is a GUI automation builder closer to a smart-home app than a programming language. Apex sits in the middle with an if-this-then-that rule language, and GHL's logic-gate programming is the most powerful but the steepest — owners switching from Apex consistently describe a hard adjustment.
Which controller has automated water testing?
Neptune: Trident automated Alk/Ca/Mg tester — $779.99 (Trident NP adds NO3/PO4). Reagent-based: ~$45 refill kit every ~2 months. HYDROS: HYDROS iV supports scheduled alkalinity testing, sampled pH, and optional salinity inputs. CoralVue also documents Maven for Alk/Ca/Mg/NO3/PO4 testing; confirm hardware requirements and current availability. GHL: ION Director — reagent-free Ca/Mg/K/Na/NO3 via ion-selective electrodes; sold in US bundles with a GHL Doser from ~$1,034. Compare the required hardware and consumables, not just the entry controller price.
Is a DIY Reef-Pi controller worth it?
Only if you're technical and enjoy the project. Reef-Pi is actively maintained open source and runs ~$150 in parts for ATO, temp, lighting and dosing control — but there's no warranty, no support, and the build is the hobby.
Is the Reef Angel controller worth it?
Yes, if you want the cheapest complete kit here ($399, relay box and probes included) and don't mind an open-source Arduino platform over a polished closed app. It's actively maintained and has real WiFi built in, but it has no automated water tester, no native dosing pump, and the smallest support ecosystem of any current option compared on this page.
Is Digital Aquatics ReefKeeper still available?
No — it's discontinued. Digital Aquatics was a side project of Dynon Instruments, which exited the aquarium-controller business entirely: no new units, no firmware updates, no support. digitalaquatics.com now redirects to a domain-parking page. Existing units generally keep running locally, but anyone buying new should look at Reef Angel (budget/DIY) or Apex/HYDROS/GHL (supported flagships) instead.

Nyos's twist-off cup design is the nicest weekly-cleaning experience in the category, and owners pay the premium for it on purpose. FAQ
Why compare on the medium-bioload rating instead of the box rating?
Because the box rating assumes a lightly-stocked tank. Manufacturers publish tiered ratings (light/medium/heavy bioload) for exactly this reason, and the medium figure is the honest one for a normally-stocked reef. A skimmer that costs less per box-rated gallon can cost more per honestly-rated gallon — the whole point of doing the math.
Are these three brands actually different, or just badges on the same pumps?
Genuinely different. Reef Octopus builds the broadest range with its own Aquatrance pumps and wins on availability and parts. Nyos is German-designed with its Quantum line's easy-service twist-off cups and strong owner loyalty at the performance end. AquaMaxx is the value line of the three, frequently undercutting comparable capacity. The table shows where each one's economics actually land.
Which one should a first-time sump owner buy?
Size first, brand second: run your true volume and stocking through our skimmer calculator, then buy whichever of these three hits your honest capacity number at the best price — that's usually an AquaMaxx or a mid-line Reef Octopus. Setup guide
120 Gallon Reef Tank: Setup, Gear List & Cost
A 120 gallon reef tank with a 48 × 24 × 24-inch footprint needs lighting planned across both its width and depth, room for a sump, and a floor checked for the loaded system. At this guide's 7× return-flow target, plan for 840 GPH delivered after head loss. The gear list totals $2,690–$4,660 for a value build or $4,660–$9,300 for mid-range gear, before livestock.
Before ordering:
measure the sump chamber, check light coverage at 24 inches of water depth, and plan freshwater storage for top-off and water changes. Use the
return pump calculator
with your actual pipe run; an 840 GPH box rating does not mean 840 GPH reaches the display.
Paid links:
if you buy through links on this page we may earn a commission, at no extra cost to you — it never affects our ratings.
How we make money
.
What the second foot of depth buys
Every smaller standard tank is a corridor — 12, 13, or 18 inches deep. At 24 inches, rockwork can stand free of the glass on all sides, corals get years of growth room in every direction, and fish that pace a 75 settle down. The same footprint-to-length ratio is why the 120 is many hobbyists' "final" tank: it's the smallest size that doesn't feel like a compromise, while still fitting a standard 4-foot space.
The logistics nobody mentions
A running 120 system weighs
~1,400–1,600 lb
loaded — on a wood floor, place it across joists, ideally near a load-bearing wall (and check, don't hope, if you're above a crawlspace). Evaporation runs 1–2+ gallons a day, so an
auto top-off
is day-one equipment, not an upgrade. And your RODI habit changes: a 75-GPD unit refilling a 120's reservoir plus water-change water spends hours running — buy 150 GPD once instead of twice.
Know your real volume first
Rock, a sand bed across 8 square feet, and the air gap take a real bite — most 120s see water volume around 100–105 gallons plus the sump. Every dose downstream keys off it:
→ get your true water volume
(the 120 is a preset).
The core gear list
Sump + return pump
A 30–40 gallon sump fits most 120 stands and gives skimmer, refugium, and ATO reservoir room to coexist. Aim for roughly
7× display turnover delivered
— about 840 GPH at the tank after head loss, which at this scale usually means a DC pump you can tune down rather than an AC pump at its limit:
→ Size your return pump with the calculator
See our full return pump rankings →
·
DC vs AC, explained →
Protein skimmer
At 120 gallons with real stocking, the skimmer is carrying serious export load — derated honest capacity matters more here than at any smaller size:
→ Find the right skimmer for your bioload
See our full protein skimmer rankings →
Lighting — where the 24″ height bites
This is the line item the depth changes. Light falls off fast through two feet of water: fixtures that comfortably grow SPS at 16–18″ of depth may only deliver softie/LPS light at a 120's sand bed. You need fixtures with a
published PAR-at-depth curve
— not a marketing "suitable for SPS" badge — and at 48×24″ of surface, plan on
two to three of them
.
Only 4 of 11 popular fixtures publish verifiable PAR curves — start there
, and check their 24″ numbers specifically.
Flow
Target
20–40× turnover
— 2,400–4,800 GPH total, more for SPS walls. The 24-inch width finally gives powerheads room to build broad, colliding gyres instead of jets; two larger units on opposing cycles beat four small ones fighting.
Work out your target and see which wavemakers actually move this much water →
Heat
Two heaters, ~200–250W each
, both on an external controller. Redundancy stops being a nicety at this investment level: one stuck-off heater still keeps the tank warm; one stuck-on heater can only push half the wattage.
Size the pair for your room →
Rock + sand
80–120 lb of rock builds real three-dimensional structure in this footprint. Sand: a 1.5″ bed across 48×24″ is about
110–140 lb
— compute your exact depth with
the volume calculator
.

The list finally opens up: most tangs (yellow, purple, tomini, even a hippo with rockwork planned for it), angel pairs, foxface, larger wrasses — alongside everything the smaller tanks allow. Setup guide
30 Gallon Reef Tank: Setup, Gear List & Cost
A 30 gallon reef tank can use rear-chamber or hang-on-back filtration without a separate sump. Plan for one reef light, a 100–150W heater with a separate controller, and 600–1,200 GPH of in-tank circulation. The equipment listed below totals $640–$1,290 for a value build or $1,290–$2,490 for mid-range gear, before livestock.
Start here:
decide between an AIO and a standard tank before buying a skimmer. Measure the rear chamber or filter clearance, then calculate
actual water volume
. The nominal 30 gallons is a planning size, not a safe dosing volume.
Paid links:
if you buy through links on this page we may earn a commission, at no extra cost to you — it never affects our ratings.
How we make money
.
Why 30 is the smallest forgiving size
Stability scales with volume. In a 10-gallon nano, a day of heavy evaporation is a measurable salinity spike; in a 30, the same day barely moves the needle. Whether it's the classic 29 (30×12×18″), a "30 breeder," or a 32-gallon AIO cube, this size holds parameters steady enough that a working adult can keep a healthy reef without checking it twice a day. It's also the cheapest entry that doesn't fight you.
Sump or no sump — the honest answer
At this size,
no sump is a legitimate choice
. All-in-one tanks (rear-chamber filtration) and hang-on-back skimmers carry a 30 comfortably at typical stocking. A sump still wins on equipment-hiding and added volume — but it roughly doubles the plumbing complexity for a tank this small. If this is your first reef, an AIO or HOB build is the version you'll actually finish.
Know your real volume first
After rock, sand, and the air gap, a "30" usually sees water in the low-to-mid 20s — which changes every dose you'll ever calculate.
→ Get your true water volume
(the 29 is a preset; AIO rear chambers count as sump volume).
The core gear list
Skimmer (or skimmerless)
A 30 with a light fish load can genuinely run skimmerless on water changes alone — that's not a compromise, it's how most nano-adjacent reefs run. If you stock normally, a compact HOB or AIO-chamber skimmer earns its keep:
→ Check which skimmers honestly fit a 30 at your bioload
See our full protein skimmer rankings →
Lighting
The one place a 30 is genuinely cheap:
one quality fixture covers it
. A 24–36″ footprint under 18″ of water means even mid-range LEDs deliver SPS-capable light at the sand.
Pick from the fixtures with verified PAR data
and spend the savings on the light you actually want.
Flow
Target
20–40× turnover
— 600–1,200 GPH total — which one well-placed small powerhead (plus the return) usually covers. In 12 inches of width, aim flow along the length, never straight at the rock.
Work out your target →
Heat
100–150W
on an external controller. In a small volume a stuck-on heater cooks the tank
fast
— the controller isn't optional at this size, it's the cheapest insurance in the hobby.
Size it for your room →
Rock + sand
20–30 lb of rock scaped open, ~30 lb of sand for a 1–1.5″ bed. Resist filling it — negative space is what makes small tanks read as mature instead of cramped.

This is the discipline size. A clown pair, a royal gramma or firefish, one goby, maybe a small blenny — and that's a

Setup guide
40 Gallon Breeder Reef Tank: Setup, Gear List & Cost
The 40-gallon breeder ("40B") is the most-recommended first reef for a reason: a wide 18-inch footprint to aquascape, low height for easy lighting, and a size that's forgiving without being expensive. Here's exactly what goes into one — and how to size each piece for
your
build, not a generic list.
Paid links:
if you buy through links on this page we may earn a commission, at no extra cost to you — it never affects our ratings.
How we make money
.
Why the 40 breeder?
At 36 × 18 × 16 inches, the 40B gives you the front-to-back depth that makes aquascaping and coral placement actually work — something taller "40-tall" or narrow tanks can't. The low height means even mid-range lights punch to the sand bed, and the ~40-gallon volume is stable enough to forgive beginner mistakes while staying cheap to stock and run. Almost every reefer who started on a nano wishes they'd started here.
The core gear list
A reef tank is a system, and each part has to match the others. Here's the short version, with the two pieces people most often get wrong linked to our calculators.
Sump + return pump
Run a sump — it hides equipment, adds water volume, and holds your skimmer. A 20-gallon long fits most 40B stands. For the return pump, aim for roughly
7× your display volume per hour at the tank
(~280 GPH for a 40B) — but the pump's box rating is measured at zero head, and your real plumbing eats a big chunk of that. Don't guess:
→ Size your return pump with the calculator
See our full return pump rankings →
Protein skimmer
The skimmer is your main filtration. Manufacturer "rated for X gallons" numbers are optimistic — they assume light stocking. For a typical mixed-reef 40B you want a skimmer that's honestly rated at your volume once derated for bioload:
→ Find the right skimmer size for your bioload
See our full protein skimmer rankings →
Lighting
Light depends on what you'll keep. Softies and LPS are happy under a single quality reef LED; a mixed-to-SPS 40B usually runs two fixtures for even coverage across the 36-inch length. Buy for the corals you want in a year, not just today. See
our reef LED lighting rankings
— only 4 of 11 popular fixtures publish real PAR data, and we name which ones.
Flow, heat, rock
Add two small powerheads for turbulent, random flow (aim for 20–40× total turnover including the return —
the flow calculator
does the math and names the pumps). A 100–150W heater on an external controller keeps things stable (
size it for your room
). Around 35 lb of dry or live rock builds your aquascape and biological base.

55 Gallon Reef Tank: Setup, Gear List & the Thing the Sale Price Doesn't Mention
The 55 is the tank everyone almost buys — it's four feet long, it's always on sale, and the number sounds substantial. Here's the honest version other guides skip: the 55 is only
13 inches front-to-back
, and that one dimension is why so many reefers regret it. We'll show you when it still makes sense, and exactly how to build one well.

The 13-inch problem, stated plainly
A reef tank is aquascaped front-to-back: rock structure, coral growth room, and open sand in front. At 48 × 13 × 21 inches, the 55 has
less
front-to-back room than a 40 breeder (18″) despite holding more water. Once the rock is in, corals grow toward the glass fast, big-bodied fish struggle to turn, and there's nowhere to put a powerhead that isn't blasting something. The extra length vs. a 40B is real — but almost everyone who reefs a 55 wishes those gallons had been shaped like
a 75
(same length, 5 more inches of depth, usually ~$100–150 more with the stand).
When a 55 still makes sense
Three honest cases: the tank is
free or nearly free
(hand-me-downs and $1/gallon sales are how most 55s happen); the stand location is genuinely too shallow for an 18-inch tank; or you're building a
fish-and-softies
display where wall-to-wall rockwork matters less. In those cases — build it well, and the length is still a real asset for wrasses and other cruisers.
Know your real volume first
A "55" typically sees water volume in the mid-40s after sand, rock, and the air gap. Pin down your true number before you dose anything:
→ get your true water volume
(the 55 is a preset).
The core gear list
Sump + return pump
Most 55s aren't drilled, so you'll either run an overflow box to a 20-long sump or skip the sump and accept a hang-on-back skimmer (a real option at this size — less capable, much simpler). If you do run a sump, aim for roughly
7× display turnover delivered
— about 385 GPH at the tank:
→ Size your return pump with the calculator
See our full return pump rankings →
Protein skimmer
The 13-inch width also squeezes the stand — check skimmer footprint against your sump before buying, not after. Rated-gallons numbers assume light stocking; derate them for a normal fish load:
→ Find the right skimmer for your bioload
See our full protein skimmer rankings →
Lighting
Same four-foot rule as the 75:
two fixtures
for even coverage. The good news is the narrow, 21-inch-tall water column is easy to light — mid-range fixtures reach the sand without breaking a sweat.
Buy from the four fixtures with verifiable PAR data
, not the marketing copy.
Flow
Target
20–40× total turnover
(1,100–2,200 GPH), but placement matters more here than in any other size — in 13 inches of width, a powerful gyre or wide-flow pump pointed wrong is a sandstorm. Two smaller powerheads angled along the length beat one big unit.

200–250W

45–65 lb

75 Gallon Reef Tank: Setup, Gear List & Cost
Ask experienced reefers what tank they'd buy again and the 75 comes up more than anything else. Four feet long, a real 18 inches front-to-back, and enough water volume that your parameters stop swinging at every mistake. Here's the full build — with each piece sized for
this
tank, not copied off a generic list.

Why the 75 is the sweet spot
At 48 × 18 × 21 inches, the 75 fixes the two things that quietly ruin smaller "starter" tanks: it has the same 18-inch front-to-back depth as the 40 breeder (so aquascaping actually works), and it stretches it across a four-foot length that fits standard lighting and gives fish real swimming room. The extra volume is stability you can't buy any other way — evaporation, temperature, and alkalinity all drift slower in 75 gallons than in 40. It's also the largest common size that still fits through a doorway on two people's arms.
Know your real volume first
A "75" doesn't hold 75 gallons — after the sand, rock, and air gap it typically sees the mid-60s, plus whatever's in the sump. Every dose and stocking decision downstream keys off that number, so pin it down first:
→ get your true water volume
(the 75 is a preset).

Sump + return pump
At this size a sump stops being optional-but-nice and becomes the default — it hides the heater and skimmer, adds 15–25 gallons of stabilizing volume, and makes an ATO trivial. A 20-long fits almost any 75 stand; a 29 fits most. For the return, aim for roughly
7× display turnover at the tank
— about 525 GPH
delivered

→ Find the right skimmer for your bioload

Four feet of tank means
two fixtures
for even coverage — a single centered light leaves the ends dim enough to matter. Softies and LPS are fine under two mid-range LEDs; SPS across a 48-inch tank is where lighting becomes the biggest line in the budget. Before you spend $700+ on marketing claims:

Guide · Nutrient export
Carbon dosing for reef tanks: nutrient export & risks
Carbon dosing adds an organic carbon source to support bacteria that consume nitrate and phosphate. The nutrients leave when you export that biomass, usually by skimming. It is a nutrient-management method, not a calcium or alkalinity supplement, and excess bacterial growth can lower oxygen. Measure nutrients, check export, and use instructions for the chosen liquid before starting.
Paid links:
if you buy through links on this page we may earn a commission, at no extra cost to you — it never affects our ratings.
How we make money
.
The one-line answer
Carbon dosing means adding an organic carbon source — vodka, vinegar, or a bottled product like NOPX — to feed bacteria that consume nitrate and phosphate as they grow. Skim off the resulting bacterial biomass (or crop it off biopellets in a reactor) and the nutrients leave with it. Start low, raise slowly, and keep your skimmer strong — the bacteria you're growing also consume oxygen, and that's the real risk here.
How it actually works
This traces back to the Redfield ratio — the roughly consistent carbon:nitrogen:phosphorus ratio found in marine bacteria and plankton across the ocean. Your tank's bacteria are typically carbon-limited, not nitrogen- or phosphorus-limited, which is exactly why nitrate and phosphate build up in the first place: there's plenty of N and P, just not enough carbon for bacteria to use it all building biomass. Add carbon, and bacterial population grows, consuming nitrate and phosphate to do it. That growing bacterial mass then needs to leave the system — via a protein skimmer pulling it out as foam, or by growing on biopellets that get cropped and replaced.
Not to be confused with Alk/Ca/Mg dosing
This is a completely different topic from what our
dosing calculator
or
kalkwasser guide
cover. Those replace what corals consume building calcium carbonate skeleton. Carbon dosing feeds bacteria to strip excess nutrients — nothing to do with calcification chemistry. Plenty of reefers run both a calcification dosing routine and a carbon dosing routine at the same time, for entirely unrelated reasons.

The ramp-up protocol
First record actual water volume, nitrate, phosphate, the chosen product and its concentration, and the label's starting instructions. Keep a record of doses and readings before adjusting. There is no single safe milliliter schedule for vodka, vinegar, and every bottled blend. Keep export and aeration working, and stop if warning signs appear. Do not use the mineral-dosing calculator to invent a carbon dose.
The real risk: bacterial bloom and oxygen crash
The bacteria you're feeding consume dissolved oxygen as they multiply — dose too much, too fast, and you can trigger a bloom that outpaces your skimmer's ability to export it, crashing oxygen levels in the process. Warning signs: cloudy water, fish breathing heavily at the surface, or a skimmer cup filling far faster than usual. Treat any of those as a stop signal, not a sign to keep pushing. If it happens: stop dosing immediately, add surface agitation or extra aeration, and do a partial water change. This is also why carbon dosing without a skimmer isn't really an option — the entire method depends on exporting the biomass you're growing, and a skimmer is how that happens.
Which method fits your tank?
Considering a DIY liquid:
choose a documented method and match its concentration exactly. A household label alone does not make a liquid suitable for a dosing schedule written for something else.
Want product-specific instructions:
compare a bottled carbon source and its ongoing cost with a documented DIY method. Follow the selected method rather than combining their dose schedules.
Considering a reactor:
plan space, flow, media maintenance, and regular nutrient checks. Biopellets do not remove the need to monitor the aquarium.
FAQ
What is NOPX (NOPOX) dosing?
Red Sea's NO3:PO4-X is a bottled carbon source used for nutrient management. It feeds bacteria; the resulting biomass must be exported. Follow that product's instructions rather than treating it as the same concentration as vodka or vinegar.
Is carbon dosing the same as the Alk/Ca/Mg dosing my calculator covers?
No — they're unrelated. Alk/Ca/Mg dosing (two-part or kalkwasser) replaces what corals consume building skeleton. Carbon dosing feeds bacteria to strip nitrate and phosphate — a nutrient-export method with nothing to do with calcification chemistry. Plenty of reefers run both at once for different reasons.
Do I need a protein skimmer to carbon dose?
Yes, effectively. Carbon dosing works by growing bacterial biomass that has to be removed from the system — a skimmer is how you export it. Without strong, healthy skimming, that biomass and the oxygen it consumes just build up in the tank instead of leaving it.
How fast should I raise my carbon dose?
Use the selected product's instructions and actual water volume; vodka, vinegar, and bottled carbon do not share one milliliter dose. Record nitrate and phosphate before adjusting. Stop dosing and add aeration if water turns cloudy or fish breathe heavily. The alkalinity, calcium, and magnesium calculator does not calculate carbon doses.

Decision guide
AC pump vs DC pump: reef return pumps compared
Choose a DC return pump for adjustable speed and feed modes; choose an AC return pump when fixed-speed operation and fewer external control parts suit the build. Neither type wins on its label alone: compare delivered flow at your head height, power draw, replacement parts, and total cost.

How we make money

AC vs DC: the short answer
DC:
speed control helps match the overflow and provides feed modes, but adds a controller and power supply to the replacement-parts list.
AC:
fixed-speed models are simpler to operate, but need careful sizing. Buy for the flow you need after plumbing losses; keep a compatible spare or a recovery plan whichever type you choose.
A 75-gallon example from our pump data
These are the smallest qualifying AC and DC pumps with recorded watts and prices in the calculator's ordered results. Both must reach 525 GPH after 4.5 ft of lift, 10 ft of pipe with a 1.029-inch inside diameter, and 4 elbows. Data date: 2026-07-01; prices have not been refreshed.

Controllability
A controllable DC pump lets you change speed without changing plumbing. Check whether the model supports feed mode and your aquarium controller before buying. A fixed-speed AC pump may allow outlet throttling, depending on its manual. Do not restrict the inlet or assume every pump responds the same way.
Noise
DC pumps are usually noticeably quieter, especially at the reduced speeds most people actually run. AC pumps hum at full tilt all the time. In a bedroom or living-room tank, that difference matters a lot more than the spec sheet suggests.
Efficiency
Compare watts at the flow your system needs. A DC model turned down may use less power than an oversized fixed-speed model, but a DC badge alone does not establish savings. Every 10W of continuous draw uses 87.6 kWh in 365 days — $14.89 at the example rate. Measure the installed draw before claiming a payback period.
Price and reliability
Check the actual model price rather than assuming AC is always cheaper. A DC controller and power supply add replaceable parts; an AC pump can still fail through wear, blockage, or restart trouble. This dataset has specifications, not a controlled failure-rate study. Test a power-off restart with your plumbing and keep strainers and impellers clean.
The failure-mode angle most people miss
If a DC controller dies, the pump stops — full stop — until you replace the controller. An AC pump has no controller to die. That's why a lot of experienced reefers run DC as their daily driver but keep a cheap AC pump boxed up as a same-day backup. Redundancy is cheaper than a tank crash.

Kalkwasser dosing, explained properly
One additive that replaces both alkalinity and calcium in a single dose, nudges pH
up
instead of down, and costs pennies a gallon in raw powder. It's also the fastest way in the hobby to crash your pH if you dose it wrong. Here's how reefers have used it safely for decades.

The one-line answer
Kalkwasser ("lime water") is a saturated solution of calcium hydroxide — Ca(OH)₂ — in RO/DI water. Dosed
slowly and matched to evaporation
, it replaces both calcium and alkalinity in one addition and helps hold pH up. Dosed too fast or too concentrated, it spikes pH hard enough to cloud your water and burn coral tissue. The chemistry is simple; the method is everything.
What kalkwasser actually does
Calcium hydroxide dissociates into Ca²⁺ and hydroxide ions (OH⁻). The Ca²⁺ is calcium, straightforwardly. The OH⁻ reacts with dissolved CO₂ and bicarbonate in your water, which raises both pH and alkalinity at the same time — a genuinely different mechanism from two-part dosing, where you're adding a carbonate/bicarbonate alkalinity source and a separate calcium chloride source that don't meaningfully move pH either direction. If your tank tends to run low pH (common in tightly sealed rooms with elevated CO₂), kalkwasser's pH lift is a real practical advantage two-part can't offer.
Our
dosing calculator
covers the two-part / DIY-additive math. Kalkwasser is the other major method — same target parameters (Alk, Ca), a different delivery mechanism.
Mixing it: the saturation limit
Mix calcium hydroxide powder into RO/DI water at roughly
1/2 teaspoon per gallon for low-demand tanks, up to 1–1.5 teaspoons per gallon for medium-to-high demand
. The practical ceiling is about
2 teaspoons (≈6g) per gallon at room temperature
— that's the solubility limit of a saturated solution. Adding more powder past that point doesn't make a stronger dose; the excess simply won't dissolve and settles as sediment. Mix, then let it sit at least 30 minutes before use so undissolved powder settles out — you want the clear solution, not the sediment.
The stirrer requirement (this is not optional)
Calcium hydroxide settles out of solution once mixed, so a static kalkwasser reservoir slowly turns back into powder at the bottom and RO/DI water on top — exactly the mix you don't want feeding your dosing line. A kalkwasser reactor solves this with a slow-turning stirrer (anything from a simple paddle to a motorized fin assembly) that keeps redistributing settled powder as the saturated solution above it gets drawn down. Run the stirrer on an intermittent schedule, not 24/7 — continuous stirring can pull too much undissolved powder into suspension and feed your tank a stronger, less predictable dose than intended.
Three ways to actually dose it
ATO-synced (the classic method):
replace your auto-top-off freshwater with kalkwasser solution instead. This is elegant because it's self-limiting — you can only add as much kalkwasser as your tank evaporates, and evaporation plus livestock consumption tend to track together reasonably well. It's also the easiest way to start: no separate pump schedule to tune.
Slow metered drip:
a dedicated peristaltic pump feeding kalkwasser continuously in small amounts spread across the day, independent of your ATO. Gives you more control over total volume than ATO-syncing alone.
pH-gated dosing:
the most precise method — a pump wired to a pH probe that only runs while pH is below a set point (a common example: on at pH 8.30, off at 8.31). This caps the dose automatically before it can overshoot. Few controllers do this natively; see our
controller comparison
for which ecosystems can pH-gate a dose (Apex with a DOS + pH probe, or GHL's Doser paired with a ProfiLux pH module) and our
dosing pump review
for standalone hardware.
The overdose risk — and how to avoid it
A dosing event should never move your tank's pH by more than about
0.2 units
. Push past that and you risk a sharp spike that precipitates calcium carbonate out of solution — you'll see the water go cloudy, and that reaction can burn coral tissue or worse. If it happens: stop dosing immediately, do a partial water change to dilute and restore chemistry, and resume at a lower rate once things stabilize. The same rule that governs our
dosing calculator
applies here — dose to a test, not to a guess, and increase gradually while tracking pH and alkalinity.
Kalkwasser vs two-part: which should you run?
Kalkwasser wins on cost (raw powder is a few dollars for months of use), simplicity of chemistry (one addition covers Alk and Ca), and the pH assist. Two-part wins on precision and scale — it doesn't need a stirrer, works with any standalone doser with zero extra hardware, and doesn't run into kalkwasser's practical ceiling: a heavily stocked SPS tank often demands more calcium and alkalinity than evaporation volume alone can carry via kalkwasser. That's why a lot of advanced reefers run
both
— kalkwasser through the ATO for baseline demand, two-part or a calcium reactor to cover the shortfall.

Once you've decided on a method, see our

— a completely different, unrelated dosing method for nutrient export.
FAQ
Is kalkwasser better than two-part dosing?
Neither is strictly better — they solve different problems. Kalkwasser is cheaper, replaces calcium and alkalinity in a single dose, and nudges pH up (useful on a tank running low). Two-part is easier to automate precisely with any standalone doser, doesn't need a stirrer, and scales further for heavy SPS demand. Plenty of experienced reefers run kalkwasser through the ATO for baseline demand and add two-part or a calcium reactor for the rest.
How much kalkwasser powder do I mix per gallon?
From 1/2 teaspoon per gallon of RO/DI for low-demand tanks up to about 2 teaspoons per gallon, which is the practical solubility limit at room temperature (a saturated solution). Adding more powder past that point does not make the solution stronger — it just leaves undissolved powder at the bottom, which is exactly what a stirrer is for.
Can I dose kalkwasser with a normal dosing pump?
You can push it through any doser, but a plain pump alone isn't the full setup — kalkwasser settles out of solution and needs continuous stirring, and pushing it in fast risks a dangerous pH spike. See our dosing pump comparison for which controllers can pH-gate a kalkwasser dose natively.
What happens if I overdose kalkwasser?
Your pH spikes, and if it climbs far enough the excess calcium and carbonate precipitate out — you'll see the water go cloudy. That precipitation reaction can burn coral tissue and, in a bad enough spike, kill corals outright. The fix if it happens: stop dosing, do a partial water change, and cut your dose rate before resuming.

Methodology
How we rate reef gear
ReefMetric exists because most reef "best of" lists are opinions dressed up as advice. Our recommendations start with numbers, and we show our work. Here's exactly how.
1. We start from published specs
Every pump, skimmer, and light in our tools is entered from manufacturer spec sheets and reputable retailer listings, with the source recorded. We convert everything to common units (GPH, feet of head, gallons) so different brands are actually comparable — a surprising amount of "which is bigger" confusion is just L/h vs GPH and meters vs feet.
2. We do the math the box won't
Specs alone mislead. A pump's "max GPH" is measured at zero head; a skimmer's "rated gallons" assumes light stocking. So our tools compute the number you actually care about:
Return pumps:
real delivered flow at
your
total dynamic head, using the Hazen-Williams friction equation plus fitting losses, solved at each pump's operating point.
Skimmers:
honest capacity for
your
bioload, using the manufacturer's own light/medium/heavy ratings where published, and a conservative derate where they only give one optimistic number.
3. We mark estimates as estimates
When a manufacturer doesn't publish enough data — a pump with no full curve, a skimmer with no bioload breakdown — we approximate, and we
flag it
(you'll see a "*"). We would rather tell you "this is a close approximation" than pretend to a precision we don't have. Where a real curve or rating exists, we use it, and those figures are exact.
4. We keep it current
Gear gets discontinued, revised, and re-priced. We update the datasets and re-check specs on a rolling basis, and date what we can. If you spot a spec that's drifted, tell us.
5. Rankings are not for sale
We earn affiliate commissions when you buy through our links, at no extra cost to you — it's how the site stays free. But the ranking is driven entirely by the data and the fit to your setup, never by which program pays more. If the best pump for your tank is a $55 one, that's what ranks first.

FAQ
An ATO replaces evaporated fresh water; it does not replace salt lost during a water change. Use the
salinity calculator
to understand your readings, and compare
reef salt mixes
separately when planning new saltwater.
Do I actually need an ATO?
Once your tank passes nano size, effectively yes. Open reef tanks evaporate roughly 1–3% of system volume per day (BRS's guideline: a 5-gallon reservoir refilled about weekly covers most tanks up to ~100 gallons) — and every gallon that leaves takes zero salt with it, so salinity climbs daily without top-off. Hand-topping works; doing it twice a day for years doesn't.
What actually fails on an ATO?
The sensor, in the "on" position. A fouled or stuck sensor keeps the pump running, which pumps your entire freshwater reservoir into the tank — crashing salinity and often flooding the floor. That's why sensor count and failsafe layers are the first column in our ranking, not the pump specs. Calcium buildup, algae, and snails sitting on the sensor are the classic triggers; clean the sensor when you clean the glass.
Optical or float sensor?
Optical has no moving parts to jam with salt creep, which is why nearly every current unit leads with one. The strongest designs pair optical with a different second technology (Tunze's float backup, Neptune's mechanical float valve) so one failure mode can't take out both layers at once.
How big should the reservoir be?
Big enough for a trip, small enough to limit the damage: if the sensor sticks, the entire reservoir goes into the tank. A 5-gallon jug on a 75-gallon system is a salinity annoyance; a 20-gallon barrel on a 50-gallon tank is a documented disaster (one owner's overnight dump dropped salinity to 1.018). Size it to about a week of evaporation.

What about kalkwasser?
None of the dosers above are purpose-built kalkwasser hardware — they're liquid dosers that can push a kalkwasser (calcium hydroxide) slurry through a line, and several are used that way. But kalkwasser needs two things a standard two-part comparison misses: a stirred reservoir (the slurry settles and needs continuous mixing or the dosed concentration drifts) and ideally pH-gated dosing (only dosing when tank pH is below a setpoint, to avoid the pH spikes kalkwasser is prone to). None of these dosers do pH-gating natively — DOS (via an Apex with a pH probe) and GHL's Doser (via ProfiLux's pH modules) are the two with a realistic path to it, since they already sit inside a broader sensor ecosystem. Budget for a stirring kalk reactor as a second purchase, not just a doser. Full mixing ratios, the stirrer requirement, and safe dosing methods:

What about nitrate and phosphate?
Every doser on this page can also run carbon dosing (vodka, vinegar, or a bottled product like NOPX) — it's the same hardware, just a different bottle. That's a nutrient-export method, completely unrelated to the Alk/Ca/Mg chemistry the rest of this page covers. See
our carbon dosing guide →
for the ramp-up protocol and the bacterial-bloom risk to avoid.
FAQ
Do I need an existing controller to use a dosing pump?
Depends which one. Red Sea's ReefDose 2/4, GHL's Doser 3 SA, Focustronic's Dosetronic, and Reef Factory's X4 are all genuinely standalone — app-controlled, no other hardware required. Neptune Systems' DOS is the exception: it's a $374.99 accessory that can't be programmed at all without a separate Apex A2 or A3 controller ($360+ more) to host it.
Can I use any of these to dose kalkwasser?
You can push kalkwasser through any of them, but a plain doser alone isn't the full setup — kalkwasser settles and needs continuous stirring, and ideally pH-gated dosing to avoid pH spikes at higher dose rates. None of these dose based on pH natively; DOS (paired with an Apex pH probe) and GHL's Doser (paired with ProfiLux's pH modules) are the two with a realistic path to it. Budget for a stirring kalk reactor as a second purchase either way.
Is the Reef Factory X4 still safe to buy?
It has the best published accuracy in this comparison (±0.01mL), but the manufacturer entered bankruptcy proceedings in 2025. It's still an active, orderable product with the company saying support continues, but long-term warranty and software support carry real uncertainty — weigh that against a financially stable brand before choosing it purely on the accuracy number.

Cost per test = kit price ÷ tests per kit, computed only where the manufacturer publishes a test count. "Not published" means exactly that — Salifert documents titration step size but no ± accuracy; treat step size as a floor on uncertainty, not a substitute for it. Salifert phosphate reports PO4-P (phosphorus), not phosphate ion — ×3.066 to compare across brands.
The catch column, spelled out
Hanna:
the cuvette technique matters — owners recommend syringe-measuring the sample rather than trusting the fill line, and the phosphate checker's reagent-powder handling is the classic source of user error. The calcium and nitrate checkers are multi-step; the alkalinity checker is the easy one.
Salifert:
the color endpoint is genuinely subjective — owner threads document ~0.4 dKH spread between readers of the same titration. Test counts are honest but consumption scales with your levels.
Red Sea:
the endpoint drifts in over ~5 drops, which is the most-complained-about readability in the category; the magnesium refill holds fewer tests than the original kit, so the refill economics are worse than the sticker suggests.
FAQ
Which parameter should I test most often?
Alkalinity. It drives coral skeletal growth, buffers pH, and moves faster than anything else you track — the standard advice is to test daily while dialing in dosing (until it holds within ~0.3 dKH for three straight days), then weekly. Calcium and magnesium drift slowly and can run on a 1–2 week cadence.
Digital (Hanna) or titration (Salifert / Red Sea)?
The real difference is who judges the endpoint. Hanna's checkers read the color with an LED and photocell — objective, repeatable, and roughly 5–10× the cost per test. Salifert and Red Sea end on a human-judged color change, which is the single most repeated complaint across owner forums: two careful people can read the same titration ~0.4 dKH apart. A common setup: Hanna for alkalinity (the high-frequency, precision-sensitive test), Salifert for everything else.
Why do two kits disagree on the same water?
Partly endpoint subjectivity, partly units: Salifert's phosphate kit reports phosphorus (PO4-P), not phosphate ion — multiply by ~3.066 before comparing it to a Hanna or Red Sea reading. Owner threads describing "wildly different readings" between brands are usually one or both of these. When kits disagree and it matters, an ICP lab test ($30–50, every few months) is the tiebreaker.
Do ICP tests replace test kits?
No — they complement them. ICP labs measure trace elements your kits can't and validate your kits' accuracy, but a 1–2 week mail turnaround can't catch an alkalinity swing that stresses coral in 48 hours. ICP quarterly, alkalinity weekly.

FAQ
How much flow do I actually need?
Bulk Reef Supply's published baseline is 20–40× your display volume per hour in total flow — softies and LPS at the low end, SPS at the top, and surveys of standout SPS tanks routinely run higher still. Your return pump counts toward the total. Our flow calculator does the math for your tank and coral type, then shows which of these pumps close the gap.
One big wavemaker or two smaller ones?
Two, almost always. Corals want chaotic, colliding flow, not a laminar river — two moderate pumps on opposing ends produce better flow than one monster, avoid a dead zone behind the single pump, and give you redundancy when one eventually needs cleaning or fails.
Why do app-controlled pumps keep failing to connect?
The most common cause isn't the pump: both Red Sea's ReefBeat and Tunze's WiFi hub only join 2.4GHz networks, so a 5GHz-only home WiFi setup fails pairing every time. AI's Nero line uses Bluetooth instead — different protocol, similar owner complaints, usually cleared by power-cycling the pump.
Are the manufacturer GPH ratings real?
They're measured maximums, not typical output — real-world flow falls with wave modes (which pulse below max by design), biofilm and coralline buildup, and age. That's one more reason to size toward the top of your target band rather than buying exactly the minimum.

The math (sourced)
The baseline is the industry's
3–5 watts per gallon
(BRS guidance), scaled by how far the room sits below the tank: a ≤5°F lift needs ~3 W/gal, ≤10°F ~5 W/gal, ≤15°F ~7.5 W/gal, and beyond that ~10 W/gal — bands cross-checked against Aqueon, Fluval, and Eheim's own sizing tables. If your number lands between two available wattages, round up.
Two heaters, not one — and always a controller
Every heater on the market — every brand, every price — has documented stuck-on failures. Two smaller heaters halve the damage a stuck-on unit can do and keep the tank warm if one sticks off; setting the second one slightly cooler makes it a true standby. And regardless of brand: put them on an independent external controller (an Inkbird ITC-306T is ~$30). The built-in thermostat is the component that fails; the controller is the second opinion that catches it.
Placement
Element in a sump chamber where the water level stays constant (the skimmer section, not the return section, which drops as water evaporates) — but the temperature
probe

Bare titanium elements (BRS's, Finnex TH/THH) have

— they heat at full power whenever plugged in. On an external controller they're arguably the most robust option; without one they're a tank cooker. The controller isn't optional with these, so compare prices with it included.

— a lightly-stocked, lightly-fed tank. Load the same tank with a full fish list and heavy feeding and that skimmer is suddenly undersized. That's why the reef rule of thumb is "buy a skimmer rated for roughly
double your display volume

derate it by your bioload
(heavy ≈ 50% of the rated number, medium ≈ 70%, light = as-rated), or use the manufacturer's own light/medium/heavy breakdown when they publish one.
Bigger isn't always better
An oversized skimmer on a lightly-fed tank can skim
too
aggressively and go unstable (constant overflowing or nothing at all). Aim for a skimmer whose derated rating comfortably covers your tank — not one rated for triple. The smallest model that clears your number is usually the right buy.

The best-rated skimmer is useless if it won't fit your sump. Two specs decide that: the skimmer's
footprint
(it needs to sit in your skimmer chamber) and its

— run it too deep or too shallow and it won't skim right. Every skimmer below lists both.
In-sump vs. hang-on-back vs. nano
In-sump skimmers are the standard for any tank with a sump — best performance and quiet. Hang-on-back (HOB) skimmers are for tanks without a sump. Nano/AIO skimmers are purpose-built for all-in-one tanks under ~40 gallons. Filter by type above to see only what fits your setup.

Dose to a test, not to a calculator.
Always confirm your levels with a reliable test kit first, add supplements to a high-flow area, and never exceed the daily limits shown. Chase one parameter at a time. When in doubt, dose less and re-test.
How reef dosing works
Corals consume alkalinity, calcium, and magnesium as they grow, and your job is to replace what's used and correct anything that's drifted. The dose is simple arithmetic — how far you're raising the level, times your water volume, times the strength of your additive — but the
safety
is in the pace. Big, fast swings (especially in alkalinity) stress and can burn coral tissue.
Raise slowly — especially alkalinity
The community-accepted ceiling is roughly
1.4 dKH of alkalinity per day
, about 50 ppm of calcium, and 100 ppm of magnesium. If your correction is bigger than that, this calculator automatically splits the total dose across enough days to stay under the limit. Rushing it is the fastest way to lose corals.
DIY two-part vs. bottled additives
Raw chemicals — soda ash or baking soda for alkalinity, calcium chloride for calcium, a magnesium mix for magnesium — are the cheapest way to dose a growing reef and are exactly what most bottled "two-part" products are. Bottled versions cost more but are premixed and convenient. Either works; pick the additive above and we'll do the math for the one you have.
Not the only way to raise Alk and Ca
This calculator covers two-part and DIY raw-chemical dosing — the most common method, and the easiest to automate with a standalone pump. It's not the only one:
kalkwasser
replaces Alk and Ca in a single dose using a completely different chemistry, and nudges pH up instead of leaving it alone. Many reefers run both — kalkwasser through the auto top-off for baseline demand, two-part to cover the rest.
Test first, every time
A dosing calculator is only as good as the number you feed it. Test with a kit you trust, enter your real current value, and re-test after dosing to confirm you landed where you expected — then set a daily maintenance dose to hold it steady.
Ready to automate it?
Once you know your numbers, a dosing pump adds them on schedule without you standing over the tank daily. See
our dosing pump comparison
— including which well-known doser can't run at all without a controller you probably don't already own. Fighting nitrate or phosphate instead? That's an unrelated dosing method — see our

PAR (photosynthetically active radiation, measured as PPFD in μmol/m²/s) is the light corals actually use. Why the box GPH is a lie
Every return pump is rated at its
maximum flow with zero head
— pump sitting next to a bucket, no plumbing. The moment you lift water up to your display and push it through pipe, elbows, and a return nozzle, flow drops fast. A pump rated "1000 GPH" can easily deliver 500–600 at a typical 4-foot rise. Sizing off the box number is the single most common return-pump mistake.
The three numbers that actually size a pump
1. Target flow (turnover).
Most reef tanks run their return at
5–10× the display volume per hour
. Mixed reefs are happy around 7×; SPS-heavy tanks push higher; fish-only can go lower. This is flow
at the tank
, after losses.
2. Static head.
The vertical distance from your sump's water surface up to the return outlet. Every foot of rise costs flow.
3. Friction (dynamic) head.
Losses from pushing water through pipe and fittings. Narrower pipe and more elbows = dramatically more loss. We compute this with the Hazen-Williams equation (C=150 for PVC) plus an equivalent-length allowance for each 90° elbow.
Total dynamic head, explained
Add static head + friction head and you get
total dynamic head (TDH)
— the real resistance your pump fights. We find each pump's
operating point
(where its flow-vs-head curve crosses your system's curve) and report the flow it truly delivers there. A pump "makes your target" only if that delivered flow meets your turnover goal.
Should you oversize?

A little, yes — pick the smallest pump that clears your target, then confirm it has a bit of headroom (and a gate valve to dial it back). Natural seawater is

Swing-arm hydrometers are cheap and notoriously off — bubbles cling to the arm, and they're calibrated for one temperature. A refractometer is the reef standard, but only if you

Conversions are linear fits anchored to natural seawater (35 ppt = SG 1.0264 = 53.0 mS/cm at 25°C) and are accurate across the reef band (~28–40 ppt); outside it, readings are flagged as extrapolated. Specific gravity everywhere here is referenced to 25°C / 77°F, the aquarium standard — a different reference temp (some lab hydrometers use 60°F) shifts SG by a few points. Salt is sold by the box, but you use it by the gallon. Two boxes at the same price can make very different amounts of saltwater, so the only fair comparison is
price ÷ gallons the box actually mixes
(at reef salinity, ~1.025). That's what we rank on here.
Your real monthly cost
Salt is the quiet recurring expense of the hobby. Your monthly cost is simply your tank volume × your water-change percentage × how often you change — times the cost per gallon of your salt. A 75-gallon tank doing weekly 10% changes goes through about 32 gallons of new saltwater a month; the salt you pick decides whether that's $10 or $25.
Cheap salt vs. reef salt
Base salts (like plain Instant Ocean) mix to near-natural-seawater levels and cost the least — great for fish-only tanks and fine for many mixed reefs that dose separately. "Reef" and "Pro" salts run elevated alkalinity, calcium, and magnesium to feed coral growth, at a higher price per gallon. For an SPS-heavy tank the elevated salt can be worth it; for softies and LPS, the cheaper salt usually is.

Why true volume matters
Every dose you calculate — alkalinity, calcium, medication — scales with water volume. Use the sticker number and you're dosing water that isn't there. The same goes for stocking decisions and salt for water changes. Get the real number once, write it on the stand, and use it everywhere:
the dosing calculator
and
the water change calculator
both want this figure, not the sticker.
The assumptions (flagged, as always)
Gallons are computed at 231 cubic inches each. Sand: dry aragonite runs about
8 lb per square foot per inch of depth
(bulk density ~96 lb/ft³, per CaribSea's spec sheets) — that's also the volume we subtract for the bed. Rock: dry reef rock is porous, so displacement varies; we estimate
1 lb displaces ~0.075 gallons
and flag it as an estimate. Dimensions are external and glass thickness is ignored, which over-counts a standard tank by roughly 2–4% — if you want to be precise, measure inside the glass.
How deep should the sand bed be?
For most reefs:
1–2 inches
. It's enough to look right, host sand-sifting critters, and stay easy to keep clean. Deep sand beds (4″+) are a deliberate filtration strategy with real maintenance implications — don't end up there by accident because a calculator told you to buy more sand. Bare-bottom is equally valid for SPS-heavy tanks chasing flow.

The math (shown, as always)
A water change of
p

p

n

One big change or several small ones?
Chemically they get you to the same place — the difference is stability. A very large change (50%+) can swing temperature, salinity, and alkalinity fast enough to stress coral, so match your new saltwater carefully or split the work across a few days. For most tanks, a series of 20–30% changes over a week or two is the calm way to knock a high reading down.

This is pure dilution math — it assumes your tank isn't
producing
more nitrate or phosphate between changes. Real tanks are. If your levels creep back up after every change, water changes are treating the symptom; the fix is export: better skimming (

for nitrate and phosphate together.

Every gallon you change is a gallon of new saltwater. Once you have your plan,
